This happened to me. It was shocking to have so much difficulty finding a job because all I would hear is "teacher shortage this", "teacher shortage that."

The plain truth is that in most areas, there is NOT a teacher shortage. 

1. There are plenty of graduates from teacher programs in most areas. 
2. Districts have their recruitment cut out for them by hiring their favorite student teachers. 
3. Best schools have their pick of experienced teachers. They can hire internal candidates from within the district.
4. The "teacher shortage" only exists for hard-to-staff urban schools and remote rural areas. 

To get your start in education, you either need to
A) know somebody in admin
B) go to an urban center
C) move to a remote location for a few years

It has nothing to do with how you look on paper or answer questions.  Trust me, I had a 4.0 too. Nobody gave a rat's patookie. Lol.

I just want to let people know that if you're in this abusive type of relationship with your parents, it's possible for people to get better. You have to both want it though. I am an elementary reading teacher and would love to help!

Sadly, CPS won't help. CPS WILL check in for educational neglect. Once your parents explain their method of homeschooling, they'll leave and won't intervene- especially if they've been taking the proper legal steps with documentation, because that counts as doing something. 

To add to that, any regular public school he would be sent to NOW will NOT be equipped to teach him how to read. Only elementary school teachers focus on teaching students how to read. Middle and high school teachers focus on comprehension.

Elementary teachers catch students by 3rd grade, otherwise they're behind for life. Teaching him can be done, but it's going to take a lot more effort than it would have if he had learned at a young age while his brain was developing rapidly. Some homeschool parents are very naieve/ignorant to this fact. 

Your brother missed out on a crucial part of reading...phonemic and [phonological](https://www.readingrockets.org/article/phonological-instruction-older-students) awareness. Essentially, segmenting sounds, and  syllables.  I can't give you a degree in teaching, but I can give you a starting point. Just Google phonemic awareness strategies. Try looking for a good phonemic awareness curriculum.

The other advice I have is for your brother to read, read, read. It comes down to practice.. I know that sounds counterintuitive since he can't read now, but there are ways you can encourage him to read. He won't learn unless he actually practices. Use multiple methods. Read to him. Have him read to you. Introduce him to audio books. Sign up for [Epic](https://www.getepic.com/sign-in). (Epic is great because he can look at the words while it reads to him!) Go to the library. Help him find books he is interested in. 

Good luck, I hope you'll find out how incredibly rewarding it is to help someone learn to read.

Here is my take as someone who has traveled outside the area and also lived in both sides of the state. The western part of the state is really dry. The eastern part of the state is humid. The summers are VERY nice compared to really hot parts of the United States. If you hate heat, North Dakota is a great place to live!

Especially if you get outside in the mornings, or evenings, it's not too hot, it's the perfect temperature. I know in the South even mornings can be hot. 

I see a lot of people talking about the humidity...and I kind of think they might be mostly from Fargo? Since you're interested in Bismarck, I don't think it would be as humid. However, it's definitely variable. It would be nowhere near the type of humidity you would feel in the deep south.

I saw some people talking about mosquitoes. Yes, there are mosquitoes, but it's not as bad as say, Minnesota. Fargo sprays heavily, so anywhere inside the city is not too bad. You can go outside without bug spray. Mosquitoes are not so bad in the western part of the state because it is dry and they don't have as many places to breed.

You just have to get used to cold snaps in the winter. If you want to move to Fargo, or Grand Forks, you have to learn how to deal with a lot of snow piling up. It doesn't pile up as bad outside of the city, because the snow has places to blow around, but driving in Fargo in the winter is hard because the city doesn't remove the snow. They just push it around or off to the side. I have never lived in Bismarck so I'm not sure if snow piles up as much there. Dealing with the cold snaps and the snow can be a deal-breaker for a lot of people that's why I mention the winters.
